"Drone sightings, drone threats including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past," Dobrindt said. "That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario," he added. "All the speculation that is currently going on about the explosives, the construction, the question of the drone, the origin and, of course, who is behind it, is now part of the investigation," Dobrindt said. The interior minister said "it would be short-sighted to believe that this form of threat, which objectively exists, can be combated or countered with simple measures. "We are dealing with a competition here which may also include foreign powers. This will be part of the investigations," he added. In June, Dobrindt created a so-called Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats, as Germany has been on high alert for espionage, sabotage and disinformation, particularly from Russia. "What is happening now also shows that the assessment made months ago — ​that we are dealing with a high level of danger — was justified," Dobrindt added. By Mattew Boyse AP AP X Story Stream recent articles Video: Global Warming Lorem Ipsum Dolor Sit ... Article: Global Warming Lorem Ipsum Dolor Sit ... Article: Global Warming Lorem Ipsum Dolor Sit ... Entry: Global Warming Lorem Ipsum Dolor Sit ... Video: Global Warming Lorem Ipsum Dolor Sit ... Prime Minister Rumen Radev can be quite pleased with his situation. His landslide in the April 19 elections gave his Progressive Bulgaria party a clear majority in parliament. Former Vice President Iliana Iotova slid into his old job and leads in the polls for the October 25 presidential election. His people are at all levels of government and his popularity remains high. No party has governed Bulgaria alone since 2001 and no politician has held such sway in the country since 1989. One hundred days after being sworn in, what Radev has been doing with this power is clearer. Corruption and State Capture Radev has shown some progress on the corruption and state capture issues that voters most want him to fix, but he is moving slowly. He quickly withdrew security from Magnitsky-sanctioned oligarch-turned-politician Delyan Peevski and former PM Boyko Borissov, both of whom many Bulgarians consider corrupt. But Radev’s MPs declined to constitute a committee to investigate Peevski, arguing it would be “just a talking shop.” Then in late July, the government presented a report on him, whereupon the National Audit Office opened an investigation, with a report due in three months. To unlock the approximately 1.4 billion Euros the EU had suspended for rule of law and other concerns, the government established an Anti-Corruption Commission and passed laws on accountability for the Prosecutor General and countering corruption. These actions freed most of the EU funds; the deadline for remaining reforms is August 31. Bulgarians will generally judge Radev on these issues. Opposition leaders have said they will support Radev if he tackles them but mobilize protests if he does not. Peevski is the litmus test but enjoys constitutional protections as a Member of Parliament. Foreign Policy PM Radev has clearly been pursuing a more independent foreign policy than his predecessors. His statements, actions, and travel indicate that he seeks maximum maneuverability within Bulgaria’s alliances as he tacks between NATO, the EU, Russia, and the United States. Radev’s first parliamentary speech highlighted sovereignty, realism, and a more “pragmatic” foreignpolicy. He downgraded Bulgarian participation at key regional formats as President Iotova skipped the Three Seas Initiative and Bucharest 9 summits. By travelling first to Berlin and Paris, Radev signaled that NATO and the EU were not his highest priorities, although Berlin remains a key reference point on the WWII-era Tsar Boris III principle “always with Germany, never against Russia.” Radev has been inconsistent with the United States, first setting impossible conditions to base aircraft for Iran operations and then agreeing until October 1. Accommodating Russia Radev accommodates Moscow more explicitly than his predecessors did. He has repeatedly called for a “new security architecture” in Europe, which would favor Russia. He declined to support a Council of Europe war crimes tribunal for Putin and studiously avoids criticizing Moscow. Radev reduced ties with Ukraine, in June stopping arms deliveries after his predecessors had sent 13 packages. His FM caused a kerfuffle by associating Bulgaria with a Ukraine-related summit declaration from which the government distanced itself. After Radev announced Bulgaria’s withdrawal from the Coalition of the Willing, his FM said Sofia was never a member. Commenting “the time for crusades is over,” Radev conditioned approval of the major 21 st EU sanctions package on dropping three Russians: Patriarch Kirill, Lukoil’s Vagit Alekperov, and businessman Iskander Makhmudov. Radev is not, however, acting like a complete “ Putin proxy .” At the NATO Ankara Summit, he sought cooperation with Ukraine on energy and drones, although offered little support. He just sent an ambassador to Kyiv after a gap of 4.5 years, and commercial arms sales continue. Radev’s approach instead is not to confront Russia, “promote peace,” and protect the Bulgarian economy. He wants it both ways: in the West, but not all-in and between East and West. But Not “Another Orban” or “Another Fico” Radev is not “ another Viktor Orban .” He has neither a parliamentary supermajority nor the ambition to lead Europe’s patriots. Bulgaria isn’t as dependent on Russian energy, and he cannot afford EU punishment. The analogy with Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico also doesn’t fully fit. Radev does not deploy Fico’s aggressive rhetoric, cultural themes and grievances, and hasn’t been as hostile to media. But Unique Instead, Radev is charting his own course. He is a unique player and is pursuing his own interests in a unique way: balancing, hedging, and engaging in transactions with partners but fully satisfying no one. Radev’s MPs call this " multi-layered diplomacy. " Others call it “multi-vector” or “multi-voiced” for messaging different audiences differently. Opposition leaders call itschizophrenia . This approach will make getting to yes with Radev challenging. He remains the weak link and complicated partner he was as president. This will make putting wins on scoreboards difficult – as with other treaty allies – but it can be done. Matthew Boyse is a senior fellow with Hudson Institute’s Center on Europe and Eurasia specializing in Central Europe. He is also an adjunct lecturer at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, the George Washington University, and American University. https://www.politico.eu/article/quebecs-.text: Quebec’s new separatist government accused Ottawa on Tuesday of barring the province from this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal and warned it would have the last word on any deals struck there that concern its powers. The dispute erupted Tuesday morning when Quebec Justice Minister Marie-Claude Sarrazin said in a statement that Ottawa had refused Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon's request to address the summit, which opens Thursday. St-Pierre Plamondon said in a post on X that the decision revealed a “serious lack of respect,” adding that Ottawa would rather he “serve shrimp cocktail” at a function rather than address one. Advertisement Advertisement Ottawa also turned down a September request from the previous Quebec government to host a reception on the sidelines of the summit, Sarrazin noted. Prime Minister Mark Carney hit back, saying St-Pierre Plamondon had himself turned down an invitation to the Thursday night summit dinner. “It’s his decision to leave an empty chair again,” Carney told reporters in French. The tiff threatens to overshadow an international gathering that Carney, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have billed as a step change in mutual relations, driven by U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariffs and scorn for the postwar Western consensus. Early drafts of the joint declaration include a digital trade deal and a pact that lets the European Investment Bank finance Canadian critical minerals projects. Many of those deliverables fall under provincial jurisdiction, such as natural resources. “'When you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu,' Prime Minister Carney told us,” Sarrazin said in her statement. “The federal government has chosen to prevent Quebec from having a say on its own territory.” Whatever agreements are signed at the summit, “Quebec is sovereign in its fields of jurisdiction internationally, so it will have the last word,” Sarrazin warned. Advertisement Advertisement Her statement evoked the 1965 Gérin-Lajoie doctrine, a principle of Quebec’s international policy that holds it can conduct its own foreign relations in areas the Canadian Constitution assigns to the provinces. It also noted that Quebec had a seat at the table during negotiations on CETA, the EU-Canada trade deal signed in 2015, attending more than 100 meetings. Yves-François Blanchet, leader of the separatist Bloc Québécois in the federal parliament, also said he had been refused a request to attend. “You’re invited to come, but above all, keep quiet. Don’t speak,” he told reporters on Parliament Hill. The plot thickens On Tuesday midmorning Ottawa time, Trump congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon on his election victory — three weeks after the actual Oct. 5 ballot — sharing an article headlined “Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney.” Trump and Carney have been at odds since the dramatic implosion of mutual trade talks in late August, with the U.S. president deploring the Canadian leader as “nasty.” The Quebec premier, meanwhile, is all-in on sovereignty in a province where support for separating from Canada reached a three-decade low of 29% earlier this year. Carney rejected St-Pierre Plamondon’s claims of exclusion, saying Quebec had been consulted on the summit. “We have had three consultations with the Quebec delegation already on the agreement with the European Union,” he said. Carney’s office told POLITICO on Tuesday that it had invited every premier to attend the Thursday dinner in Montreal. Advertisement Advertisement St-Pierre Plamondon also skipped a federal meeting with Indigenous leaders and premiers on Monday, an absence Carney criticized. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the premier was “welcome” in Montreal, but that the summit was a federal meeting, with geopolitics a federal area of responsibility. “With everything going on in the world, we just need to make sure we can reach an agreement with the European Union,” she said. “That’s what Quebecers want.” Despite the public spat over the summit logistics, working-level officials described the relationship between the different levels of government as constructive. Hélène Drainville, Quebec’s delegate general in Brussels, told POLITICO on Monday that federal and provincial officials have set up joint working groups to implement the summit’s outcomes. Quebec is also in talks with the European Investment Bank and DG GROW, the Commission’s industry department, about the bank’s entry into Canada, she said. “Right now, all the signals are green,” Drainville said. She underlined, however, that the province “has to be at the table” if Ottawa and Brussels strike deals in its areas of jurisdiction. Mickey Djuric and Sue Allan contributed reporting from Ottawa.
